name: Leave-in conditioner

card.summary: A no-rinse conditioner for daily softness, slip and frizz control; the effects are cosmetic and temporary.
card.note: Cosmetic coating only; buildup is reported if overused or applied to the scalp.

quick.overview:
A leave-in conditioner is applied to damp hair after washing and not rinsed out. It is meant to keep hair softer, smoother and easier to comb between washes, and some versions add heat protection.

It works on the surface of the hair, as encyclopedic sources say hair cannot be repaired biologically. No trials of the product category were found.
quick.mechanism: Light conditioning agents, usually cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants and oils, coat the fibre, flatten the cuticle, reduce friction and static, and leave a thin film that persists until the next wash.
quick.risks: Considered a low-risk cosmetic. Buildup and scalp flaking are reported with heavy use or application at the roots, and product guidance advises applying to lengths and ends. Individual ingredients can cause allergic reactions.

lead: A leave-in conditioner is a no-rinse hair product applied to damp (or sometimes dry) hair after washing and left in. People use it to make hair look smoother, shinier and more controlled through the day: less frizz and static, easier combing and styling, and in some formulas protection from heat tools. For anyone working on hair as part of their overall look, it is a quick way to improve how the hair lies and reflects light.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes leave-in conditioners as lighter than rinse-out types, often containing silicones or polymers that reduce static and may give some heat and UV protection.[2] Conditioners in general improve combability and appearance by reducing friction between fibres; they coat the hair rather than repair it, since the hair shaft is not living tissue.[2] Formats include creams, lotions, sprays and mists.[1]
No clinical trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were found; the published research on conditioning agents is mostly laboratory testing of individual ingredients.[2]

chain: Light conditioning film stays on the hair shaft
Less friction, static and frizz; smoother cuticle surface
Hair looks shinier, softer and easier to style
angle.text: A leave-in coats the hair with conditioning agents that flatten the cuticle and reduce friction, so hair appears smoother and shinier and detangles with less breakage. The effect lasts until the next wash.

infobox: Cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants, oils, proteins

paras: Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, lists typical ingredients as humectants such as glycerin, silicones such as dimethicone, plant oils such as argan or jojoba, proteins and vitamins.[1] Wikipedia's article on conditioners names cationic surfactants (such as cetrimonium chloride), fatty alcohols, silicones, hydrolysed proteins, panthenol, humectants, acidifiers, sequestrants, UV filters and thermal protectants as typical components of conditioners generally.[2]

Wikipedia explains that undamaged hair has a hydrophobic lipid film on its cuticle, and that weathering, bleaching, dyeing and heat styling strip it and leave a more hydrophilic, negatively charged surface. Cationic surfactants bind to that surface with their hydrophobic tails facing outward, which flattens the cuticle scales, reduces static and flyaways and gives oils and silicones something to bond to.[2] Damaged hair carries more negative sites and so absorbs more conditioner.[2]

Rinse-out conditioners are the most common type, applied after shampooing and rinsed after a few minutes, while leave-ins stay in the hair.[1][2] Deep conditioners or hair masks are thicker and are left on for about 20 to 30 minutes.[2] Leave-in formulas are described as lighter so they do not weigh hair down, and some products include UV filters, chelating agents for hard water or thermal-protectant polymers aimed at heat tools above 200 degrees Celsius.[1][2]

Wikipedia notes that people have used natural oils on hair for centuries. Macassar oil, a scented dressing sold from the 1790s by London barber Alexander Rowland, was widely used by men through much of the 19th century, and its greasy residue led to washable antimacassar covers around 1850.[2] Modern conditioner is commonly dated to about 1900, when Edouard Pinaud presented Brilliantine at the Paris Exposition, a claim the article flags as uncited. Silicones, fatty alcohols, quaternary ammonium compounds and polymers later replaced simple oils.[2]

Manufacturers and secondary sources describe less frizz, easier combing, reduced breakage, added shine and some protection from heat styling.[1] Wikipedia notes that benefits such as repair and strengthening are often advertised but are not treated as established.[2] Laboratory studies it cites include reduced combing breakage after certain polymer pretreatments before hot flat-ironing and increased break stress with panthenol in one study.[2]

Product guidance summarised by Grokipedia advises applying leave-ins to mid-lengths and ends and avoiding the scalp to prevent buildup or irritation, and says dermatologists recommend washing out accumulated residue periodically.[1] Wikipedia notes that conditioner left on the scalp can dry and flake in a way that resembles dandruff.[3]
No studies found. No human trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were located; related evidence consists of ingredient-level laboratory studies of conditioning agents.[2]

timeline.event: London barber Alexander Rowland begins selling Macassar oil, a scented hair dressing.[2]
Edouard Pinaud presents Brilliantine at the Paris Exposition, commonly cited as the start of modern conditioner (uncited in Wikipedia).[2]
